name: Novice fundamentals
description: Your first two or three months, before any of it needs to work against resistance: how to be safe, how to move, and a map of where you are. Everything here completes from showing up and drilling — no live rounds required — so it finishes while a belt roadmap is just getting started.

phases.title: Being a good training partner
phases.description: Nothing in jiu-jitsu is worth an injury — yours or theirs. This is the material every good academy teaches first, and the only part of the sport you are expected to be good at on day one.

items.title: Where this sits
items.notes: This comes before the white belt roadmap, not instead of it. It finishes in your first two or three months and every item completes from showing up and drilling — no live rounds required. When it is done, open the white belt roadmap: that one teaches the map of the sport and one answer from every place on it.

items.title: Tap early, tap often
items.notes: A tap is information, not defeat: it says the position was lost ten seconds ago and you now know why. Tap physically on their body, tap loud, and say it if your hands are trapped. Recognise your partner's taps the same way — verbal, physical, or a stopped struggle.

items.title: Protect the people you train with
items.notes: Control your body weight, put submissions on slowly, and let go the moment they tap. Know what is off-limits for beginners at your academy — typically heel hooks, neck cranks and slams — and keep it off-limits even when one is offered to you.

items.title: Mat etiquette
items.notes: Clean gi, short nails, no shoes on the mat, shoes everywhere else. Tell the coach about skin problems before they become the whole academy's problem. Start rounds on time, don't coach mid-roll, and assume everyone is having a harder week than you.

phases.title: The movements under everything
phases.description: Every escape and every sweep is built out of half a dozen movements. Drill them until they stop costing attention — the criteria here count classes drilled, not wins, because a movement pattern is earned by repetition across weeks, not by one good night.

items.notes: Falling is the first skill: chin tucked, arms slapping, never a hand posted behind you.
The fall you actually take from most throws. Same rule: the mat takes the impact, not your wrist.
Over the shoulder, not the head — the roll that turns being pushed into repositioning.
The hip power behind every mount escape. Heels close, bridge to a shoulder, not straight up.
The one way to stand up that doesn't give your legs away while you do it.
Hips down and back the moment someone shoots — the difference between defending a takedown and reacting to one.
Base, balance and posture while moving. Everything standing starts from here.

phases.title: The map
phases.description: Jiu-jitsu makes no sense as a list of moves and complete sense as a map of positions. Learn the map first: where you are, what it is worth, and which way is up.

items.title: The positional hierarchy
items.notes: From best to worst for the person in control: back control, mount, knee-on-belly, side control, north–south, half guard, guard, turtle, standing. Every roll is both people trying to climb this ladder at once — most of what looks like chaos is just two climbs colliding.

items.title: Top and bottom are different games
items.notes: On top you pass, pin and attack; on the bottom you frame, escape and recover guard. Guard is the one bottom position that is not losing — your legs are between you and them, and that is a weapon.

items.title: Position before submission
items.notes: The oldest rule in the sport and the one under every other. Control where the fight is before you spend anything on a finish — a submission attempted from a bad position usually costs the position and lands nothing.

items.title: Connection, frames and inside position
items.notes: Frames are bones placed where their weight wants to go — a forearm at the neck, an elbow inside a knee. Inside position means your arms and knees are between their limbs, not around them. Whoever owns the inside owns what happens next.

phases.title: Survive first
phases.description: Before anything can be attacked, the bad places have to stop being emergencies. Drill the survival postures until being pinned is merely uncomfortable — the escapes themselves belong to the white belt roadmap; this is the part that keeps you safe while you learn them.

items.title: The defensive sequence
items.notes: In order, always: protect your neck, bring your elbows in, build frames, restore your alignment, make space, recover guard or get on top. Skipping ahead — reaching for an escape before the neck and elbows are safe — is how survivable positions become submissions.
Elbows connected to knees, hands guarding your neck. Mount stops being terrifying the day this becomes automatic.
A forearm at the neck and a frame at the hip. You are not escaping yet — you are making their pin cost something.
Chin down, hands win the fight over your collar. Losing your back is a position lost, not a round lost — as long as your neck stays yours.

name: White belt: learn the basic game
description: Goal: understand what is actually happening in a BJJ match, and have a basic answer from every major position. White belt is position, safety, escapes and a small number of dependable techniques — not a large collection of them. The eleven milestones follow a match from its beginning: standing, to the ground, guard, the sweep or the pass, the pins, the back, the turtle, and then how to get out of all of it. The shape to hold in your head: standing → takedown or guard pull → guard → sweep or pass → side control → mount or back → submission; and when position is lost, escape → recover guard or get on top → start attacking again. Milestones complete from what you log live. Nothing here can be ticked off by hand.

phases.title: Start Standing
phases.description: Learn how to safely begin an exchange. Nothing in this section scores a point and all of it decides whether the rest of the round happens on your terms.

items.notes: Knees bent, back straight, weight between your feet — the posture everything else is played from.

items.title: Base and balance
items.notes: Being hard to move is a skill before it is a technique. Weight through the whole foot, hips underneath you, and never let your feet cross or your head travel past your knee.
In the gi, a collar and a sleeve is worth more than being stronger.
Whoever gets their hands inside decides what happens next.
Learn to land before you learn to be thrown. The backward breakfall is the same skill on the other axis — drill both.
How you get up without giving away your back or your legs.
The answer to a leg attack, and the first thing to drill until it is a reflex.

phases.title: Get the Fight to the Ground
phases.description: Know a few simple ways to initiate. The goal is not to know ten takedowns — a white belt should have two or three they understand well, and should recognise the rest when they are being done to them.

items.notes: The one everybody learns, and it still works.
The other half of the pair — they defend one by giving you the other.
No level change, no scramble, and it travels to no-gi.
A foot sweep costs nothing when it fails, which is what makes it worth trying often.
What their bad posture is for.
Pulling guard is a decision, not a surrender — but only if you choose the position you land in.

phases.title: Understand Guard
phases.description: Learn what guard is and why it matters. The thing that makes a guard a guard, rather than being underneath somebody, is that your legs are between you and them.

items.notes: The first guard, and the one that teaches posture-breaking.
Open guard starts with the hands, not the feet.
Half guard is a position with its own fight, not a failed guard.
The close-range guard, and the one that lifts.

items.title: Keep opponent between your legs
items.notes: Every guard is one answer to a single question: are your legs still between you and them? The moment they are not, you are not in guard — you are being passed.

items.title: Control distance
items.notes: There are two safe distances and one dangerous one. Far enough that their weight is off you, or close enough that they cannot build a base. The middle is where you get passed.

items.title: Break posture
items.notes: A posture-broken opponent cannot pass, cannot strike and cannot see. Breaking it is worth more than any single attack, because every attack comes after it.

items.title: Protect yourself
items.notes: Elbows in, hands in front of your neck, chin down. Most of what goes wrong from the bottom starts with an arm that drifted away from your body.

items.title: Create angles
items.notes: Square-on, they have all their weight and both arms. Off to one side, half of that is gone. Almost everything that works from guard begins by getting off the centre line.

phases.title: Sweep From Bottom
phases.description: Learn how to get from bottom to top. The important concept: if you cannot submit safely, improve your position — and a sweep is how that is done from underneath.

items.notes: The first one most people land in a live round.
When they sit back to open your guard, the space they made is the sweep.
The flower sweep and the pendulum are one movement; it takes the arm with it.
Distance guard, standing opponent — the one that works when they stand up.
Close range, hooks in, and the whole body does the work.
The half-guard underhook, cashed in.

phases.title: Pass the Guard From Top
phases.description: Understand that before attacking, you usually need to get past the legs. The main concept is the order: legs, then hips, then shoulders, then control.

items.notes: You cannot pass a closed guard; you open it first, and standing is the safest way.
The pass that works in both gi and no-gi and never stops working.
Move their legs rather than your own weight.
When you cannot go around the legs, pick them up and stack.
The slow one, and the one nobody enjoys being underneath.
Half guard is where most passes stall — this is how they finish.

phases.title: Establish Side Control
phases.description: Learn how to actually hold someone after passing. A pass is not finished until the pin is, and the pin is what every attack in this section is launched from.

items.notes: The crossface turns their head away from you, and their hips have to follow it.

items.title: Underhook
items.notes: The far underhook is what stops them turning in and rebuilding a guard. Crossface on one side, underhook on the other — that pair is the pin.

items.title: Hip control
items.notes: Your hips stay low and off theirs, not resting on them. Weight on their chest and shoulders, space where their hips are, so there is nothing for them to shrimp against.

items.title: Chest-to-chest pressure
items.notes: Pressure is chest on chest, not arms braced on the mat. If you are holding yourself up, you are holding yourself up — they are free.

items.title: Prevent guard recovery
items.notes: Everything they do from here is an attempt to get a knee or an elbow back in front of you. Block the knee line and the escape has nowhere to go.
The pin is a place you leave, and mount is the usual next stop.
Lighter, more mobile, and it makes them give you something.
Trap the near arm across their own neck and the back is already half taken.
The first submission most people ever finish, and it is right there in the pin.
The far arm is an attack that starts from the pin you already hold.
When they push into you with the near arm, they have handed it over.
Their own shoulder does the choking, which is why it works without much strength.

phases.title: Establish Mount
phases.description: Learn to stabilize before attacking. Chasing a submission from an unstable mount is how you end up back in their guard.

items.notes: Knees near the hips, weight forward. Low mount is where you survive their first bridge.
When they turn on their side, you climb. High mount is where the attacks live.
The position mount becomes every time they turn away — not a mistake, a stop on the way to the back.
Ride the bridge rather than fighting it. Posting into the roll is what makes their escape fail.
Holding the pin is not the end of the round — the arm they push with is the arm you take.
The same choke as from side control, arrived at from the other side.
The oldest choke in the gi, and it still catches blue belts.
The one they never see, because it needs almost no space.
When the collar choke makes them push, the armbar is already there.

phases.title: Take and Control the Back
phases.description: Understand why the back is one of the strongest positions: they cannot see you, they cannot reach you, and everything you do from here they have to defend blind.

items.notes: One arm over the shoulder, one under the armpit, hands joined. Without it there is no back control.
The hooks keep you attached while they turn. They are not what holds them — the seatbelt is.

items.title: Chest-to-back connection
items.notes: Your chest stays glued to their back. The moment a gap opens they can slide down and put their shoulders on the mat, which is the whole escape.

items.title: Head position
items.notes: Head on the same side as your choking arm, jaw tight to their shoulder. Heads on opposite sides is how you get rolled over the top.
Back control is followed, not held. When they slide out, you go with them.
The one submission that needs no gi, no leverage and no strength advantage.
The gi's version, and it arrives before they know it started.

phases.title: Turtle
phases.description: Know what to do from both sides. Turtle is a door rather than a home — it is where scrambles pause, and staying still in it is volunteering your back.

items.notes: Neck first, always. Everything else is negotiable.
Elbows to knees, no space underneath. A hook cannot go where there is no room.
The wrestler's answer, and the fastest way out of the position.
Roll across the shoulders, thread the legs back through, and you have a guard again.
Sometimes the guard you recover is half of one, and that is fine.
If nothing is holding you down, stand up. It is allowed and it is often best.
From the top, the seatbelt comes before anything else — same grip, same reason.
Break them down to one side and the turtle stops being a shell.
The first hook goes in on the side your chest is already on. Chasing the far one is what gets you rolled.
The turtle's real punishment: you end up on the back with both hooks in.

phases.title: Escape Bad Positions
phases.description: One of the most important white belt areas, and the one that decides whether training is enjoyable. The order never changes: survive, then escape, then recover — and rejoin the round where you left it.

items.notes: When someone mounts you and reaches for something, you can put them underneath you.
The escape that works when they do not give you the roll: elbow, knee, half guard, guard.
You can turn frames into space and get your guard back.
When the guard is not coming back, go the other way and come up.
Half guard counts as recovering guard. It is a position, not a consolation.
Two hands on one arm, chin buried. Nothing else matters until the choking arm is controlled.
The two-on-one is the grip that makes the rest of the escape possible.
One hook removed is half the control gone.
Get both shoulders to the floor and their back control has become a bad side control.
Turn into them, not away. Turning away is how the choke finishes itself.
Compact, neck covered, no space for a hook. From here you have time to choose.
The sit-out that ends facing them, with a guard back between you.
Standing back up is an escape, and often the best one available.

phases.title: Submission Defense
phases.description: Understand the danger before learning advanced attacks. These eight are what you will actually meet, and knowing the defence is what lets you train hard without getting hurt. Tap early — a defended submission and an injured joint are seconds apart.

items.notes: Chin to the elbow crease, both hands on the choking wrist, before the grip closes.
Shoulder into the neck, head to the choking-arm side. Standing works only while their legs are open.
Posture and the angle. Pulling the arm out before you have either is what finishes it for them.
Thumb up, elbow away, hands joined, stack. Once the arm is straight and the hips are up, tap.
Shorten the lever and turn toward the trapped arm, never away from it.
Straighten the arm and the lock has nothing to bend.
Turn toward the trapped arm before they walk past your head. It is a race against the walk.
Boot the foot, sit up toward the lock, hand-fight the grip down. Rolling away is what finishes it.

name: Blue belt: build reliable systems
description: Goal: stop thinking only in individual techniques and start understanding technique → opponent reaction → second technique. A blue belt should begin developing a real personal game. The ten milestones follow the same match order white belt learned, one layer deeper: chains instead of single attacks, retention before attacking, two guards that answer each other, passing and pinning as systems, and escapes that become combinations. The shape to hold in your head: standing combination → takedown or guard entry → your preferred guard → sweep, submission or wrestle-up → passing system → pin → advance position → submission chain → they escape → follow them into another attack. Milestones complete from what you log live.

phases.title: Standing
phases.description: Build reliable combinations rather than single attacks. Start chaining: single leg → they defend → double leg. Snapdown → front headlock → go behind.

items.notes: The grip fight decides which of the attacks below is even available.
The inside single is the one that chains, because it puts you on the centre line.
What their single-leg defence hands you.
The third entry off the same level change.
No level change and nothing to sprawl on.
Their posture is the opening, and this is what it opens into.
The cheapest back take in the sport, and it starts standing.
A foot sweep is what makes them stop moving forward.
If you pull, pull into something. Landing in a guard you play is the whole point.

items.title: Attack in twos
items.notes: Every attack above has a defence, and every defence opens the next one. Single leg → they sprawl → front headlock. Snapdown → they post → go behind. Learn the pair, not the move.

phases.title: Guard Retention
phases.description: Before becoming great at attacking guard, become difficult to pass. Losing a rung of this ladder is not losing the guard — it is moving to the next answer down.

items.notes: The inside space is the guard. Frames are how you keep it.
The movement every recovery below is built from.

items.title: Inside position
items.notes: Feet, knees, hands and elbows: whoever is inside decides. Retention is a pummelling contest with four limbs rather than two.
Legs pummel like arms do, and whoever gets inside keeps the guard.
Frame the biceps, get the shin back in front of the cutting knee — or take the underhook and come up.
The toreando beats you on speed, so the answer is rotation rather than pushing.
The window is before their weight arrives. Flat is what gives up the back.
From seated, the reset is the skill — you rebuild before they arrive.
Supine, the hips go the other way, and the guard comes back on the far side.

phases.title: Build Two Guards
phases.description: Start developing at least two connected guards, so that when one is shut down the other is already there. The pairs that work: butterfly and half guard; De La Riva and single leg X; collar sleeve and lasso; seated guard and shin-to-shin.

items.notes: Close range, both hooks in, and everything lifts.
The other half of the first pair, and the one that survives pressure.
The open guard that hooks rather than frames.
How De La Riva and the ashi family connect — one entry, two guards.
The gi guard that costs them their posture and their far arm at once.
Its partner: when the collar sleeve is cleared, the lasso is already set.
Seated is a guard, not a pause. It begins with the hands.
The connection between seated guard and every leg entry below it.

items.title: Two guards that answer each other
items.notes: The point of a pair is that the passer's answer to one puts them in the other. If your second guard needs a reset to reach, it is not a pair — it is two separate games.

phases.title: Attack From Guard
phases.description: Build combinations rather than isolated moves. Each of the three chains below is one grip and several exits: defending the first is what opens the next.

items.notes: When they leave an arm in and posture up, it is already there.
The triangle defence is the armbar entry.
And when they pull the arm back out, the shoulder is the third exit.

items.title: Closed guard: triangle ↔ armbar ↔ omoplata
items.notes: One system with three exits. Learn the triangle first, then notice the armbar was always there every time they pulled the arm out, and the omoplata every time they pulled it back in.
The hook sweep is the threat that makes the arm drag work.
They post to stop the sweep, and the post is the drag.
And the drag's destination: climbing to the back rather than settling for the sweep.

items.title: Butterfly: sweep → arm drag → back take
items.notes: Threaten the elevation, take the reaction. Nobody defends a butterfly sweep without giving you an arm.
The underhook, taken from the knee shield before they flatten you.
What the underhook becomes once you come up on it.
From the dogfight, the sweep is a matter of which way they lean.
And when they whizzer instead, the arm comes out and the back is there.

items.title: Half guard: underhook → dogfight → sweep → back take
items.notes: One underhook, three destinations. Which one you get is decided by them, not by you — which is the whole idea of a chain.

phases.title: Develop Passing Systems
phases.description: Two families, and a blue belt needs one of each. Start combining them: toreando → they recover → knee cut → they block → leg drag.

items.notes: Movement passing starts here: their legs move, not your weight.
The one that works everywhere, and the hinge of every chain below.
The cross-step that beats a guard playing for distance.
Where movement passing ends up, and the fastest route to the back.
Pressure passing: slow, heavy, and nobody enjoys being underneath it.
Take the hips away and the guard has nothing left to retain with.
When you cannot go around, pick them up and stack.
Half guard pressure is where most passes stall and where this one finishes.

items.title: Combine them
items.notes: A pass that fails is a reaction you asked for. Toreando to make them turn in, knee cut to make them block, leg drag into the space the block made.

phases.title: Control After Passing
phases.description: Become better at preventing escapes. Connect the pins instead of holding one forever — side control → north-south → knee-on-belly → mount → back.

items.notes: The pin you arrive in, and the one everything else leaves from.
The head switch that answers their first frame.
Lighter and more mobile, and it makes them give you something.
When their frames go to your hips, the mount is on the other side of them.
And when they turn instead, the back is already exposed.

items.title: Instead of holding one position forever
items.notes: A pin is not a destination, it is a place you leave when they react. The athlete who transitions on every frame is much harder to escape than the one who squeezes harder.

phases.title: Build Submission Chains
phases.description: Three chains, one per position. In each, the defence to the first attack is the entry to the second.

items.notes: The mount chain starts with the choke that makes them turn.
They turn away from the choke, and the gift wrap takes them to the back.
Where every one of these chains is trying to end up.

items.title: Mount: arm triangle → back take → RNC
items.notes: Nobody escapes the arm triangle by staying flat. The turn that saves the neck is what hands you the back.
The side control chain starts with the grip that outlives the position.
They straighten the arm to save the shoulder, and the elbow is there.
And when they roll away from both, the kimura grip goes with them.

items.title: Side control: kimura → armbar → back take
items.notes: One grip, three answers. The kimura is worth learning as a control before it is worth learning as a finish.
From the back, the answer when the hand fight denies you the RNC.
And when both hands go to the neck, the arm is unattended.

items.title: Back: RNC → short choke → armbar
items.notes: Their two hands cannot be in three places. Every defence from the back gives up one of the other two attacks.

phases.title: Front Headlock
phases.description: Begin treating the front headlock as a major attacking position rather than a place a scramble passes through.

items.notes: The seated snapdown: the front headlock is available from the bottom too.
The chin strap is what makes it a position instead of a grab.
The default, and the one to reach for first.
The high-elbow finish, when the go-behind is denied.
The arm-in version, which finishes on the shoulder rather than the throat.
When they turn in toward you, the near arm is already threaded.
And when they turn away, the roll takes them with it.
The other exit: when nothing finishes, take the back and start again.

items.title: The go-behind is the default
items.notes: Chase the choke first and you will be given up on the position when it fails. Chase the position and the chokes arrive on their own.

phases.title: Leg Locks
phases.description: Understand the fundamental leg-lock game — the positions first, one submission, and the safety rules that make training this survivable for both of you.

items.notes: Straight ashi: the first entanglement, and the one every other is described against.
Single leg X, where the sweeps and the ankle lock share an entry.
Outside ashi, and the moment the knee line starts to matter.
50/50, introduced — a position both of you are in at once.
The one submission here that is legal at every belt in every ruleset.

items.title: The knee line
items.notes: Whose knee is past whose decides who is attacking. Learn to read it before you learn any finish — it is the difference between a leg lock and a leg tangle.

items.title: Control before submission
items.notes: The same rule as everywhere else, and it matters more here because the failure mode is a knee rather than a lost point. Position, then the finish.
The safe escape: clear the knee line and come up, rather than rolling out of it.

items.title: Hand fighting
items.notes: Their grip on your foot is the whole submission. Fighting the hands is what buys the time to clear the entanglement, and it starts before you are caught.

phases.title: Improve Escapes
phases.description: White belt escapes become combinations. The blue belt should understand escape chains: elbow escape → they block → bridge → they post → recover half guard.

items.notes: The first link, and the one they will be ready for.
What their block hands you.
And the chain itself, run end to end without stopping to reset.
The same idea one position over: frame, push, and take whichever exit opens.
The last link that matters, because the alternative is a nap.

items.title: Escape chains, not escapes
items.notes: A single escape is a thing they can prepare for. Two escapes that answer each other's defence cannot be blocked at the same time, which is the same insight as the attack chains three milestones up.

name: Purple belt: connect the entire game
description: Goal: stop seeing BJJ as separate positions. The question stops being "what do I do from here" and becomes "what reaction do I want them to give me". Most of this belt is systems, flows and strategy rather than new techniques, so most of what follows is written rather than counted — that is deliberate, and the milestones that do carry techniques are the ones where a specific thing has to work. The shape to hold in your head: create your preferred starting exchange → force your A-game position → create a reaction → they defend → transition to the secondary system → pass, sweep or back take → control → create a submission dilemma → they escape → use the escape to enter the next position → continue the chain.

phases.title: Establish a Standing Game
phases.description: Have a clear starting strategy. Grip fight → single leg → they sprawl → front headlock → guillotine or back take. Or: guard pull → immediate sweep attack. A purple belt should rarely begin a match without knowing what they want.

items.notes: The finish that answers the sprawl instead of abandoning the leg.
Where the failed single leg is supposed to arrive.

items.title: Guillotine
items.notes: One of the two exits from the sprawl, and the one they expect. The technique itself is milestone 7's, where the front headlock is built as a system rather than met as an outcome.

items.title: Back take
items.notes: The other exit, and the one that scores without risk. Also milestone 7's — what matters here is having decided which of the two you are hunting before the shot goes in.
If the answer is to pull, pull directly into an attack.

items.title: Know what you want before it starts
items.notes: Every exchange above is chosen, not discovered. The purple belt's advantage over the blue belt is rarely a better single leg — it is having decided what the sprawl was going to turn into before shooting.

phases.title: Build an A-Game Guard
phases.description: Choose a primary guard — butterfly, half guard, De La Riva, collar sleeve, lasso, X guard or a wrestle-up guard — and know six things about it rather than one.

items.title: Choose one, and mean it
items.notes: A guard you play in every round beats three you play sometimes. The choice matters less than the commitment: the depth is what makes it an A-game, not the guard.

items.title: How to enter it
items.notes: From standing, from a pull, from a failed pass, from a scramble, and from underneath a pin. A guard you can only start a round in is not yet a system.

items.title: How to retain it
items.notes: What is your answer when the first grip is stripped? An A-game guard has a second and a third configuration, not one.

items.title: How to sweep from it
items.notes: At least two, going in different directions, so their base cannot answer both.

items.title: How to submit from it
items.notes: One real threat, so the sweeps are not the only thing to defend.

items.title: How to take the back from it
items.notes: The exit that is worth more than the sweep, and the one most guards have and few people build.

items.title: What to do when it is shut down
items.notes: The honest question, and the one milestone 4 exists to answer. Every guard has a passer who beats it — the plan for that day is part of the guard.

phases.title: Build Guard Connections
phases.description: Move between guards naturally. Seated guard → shin-to-shin → single leg X → X guard → sweep. Or: De La Riva → reverse De La Riva → kiss of the dragon → back take.

items.notes: The first connection, and the one that teaches the idea.
Underneath them, and the sweep is a formality once you arrive.
Where the first chain ends: on top, with their leg already dragged.
The second chain's hinge, and the guard most people skip.
And its exit — under and behind, rather than over the top.

items.title: Guards are one position with several shapes
items.notes: A blue belt has two guards and switches between them. A purple belt has one guard that changes shape as the passer moves, which is why nothing is ever reset.

phases.title: Advanced Guard Retention
phases.description: Recover during late-stage passes, not just early ones. This is the milestone that decides whether the A-game guard above is a game or a preference.

items.notes: Still the foundation, and still the thing that fails first when it is neglected.
Upside down is a position, not an emergency.
The roll that gets the legs back in front from almost anywhere.
The same movement from turtle, which is where late recoveries actually start.
When the shoulder line is gone, the leg goes over the top.
Half guard is a recovery, not a failure — and it goes all the way back.
Before the hips connect, or not at all. Once the lock closes it is a pin escape.
The drag is the hardest of the three to recover from, because it is already past you.

phases.title: Build a Passing Tree
phases.description: Instead of knowing passes, create reactions. Knee cut → they block the knee → back step → they follow → leg drag → they turtle → back take.

items.notes: The first branch: what the blocked knee cut becomes.
The back step, which is the branch nobody defends because it goes backwards.
And the branch that ends the tree, because they cannot turtle out of it.

items.title: A pass is a question
items.notes: Every pass in the tree is a question with two answers, and you have prepared both. The passer who is surprised by the defence has a list; the passer who was waiting for it has a tree.

phases.title: Control Transitions
phases.description: Move without giving space. Side control → north-south → kimura → they turn → back → they escape the back → mount. BJJ becomes circular rather than linear.

items.notes: The grip that survives the transition, which is why the chain starts here.
Their turn away from the kimura is the back take.
And a back escape is not an escape if you are already mounting them.

items.title: Circular, not linear
items.notes: A linear game ends when the last position is escaped. A circular one has no last position: every escape is an entry into the position before it, so there is nothing to run out of.

phases.title: Develop Submission Systems
phases.description: Three systems, each one grip or one position with several finishes hanging off it. Every lesson below is one the document names, in the order it names them.

items.notes: Front headlock: the finish the position is named for.
When they turn in toward you, the near arm is already threaded.
And when they turn away, the roll takes them with it.
The exit that is not a choke, and the highest-percentage one in the family.
Kimura: the grip, taken as a control rather than reached for as a finish.
They straighten the arm to save the shoulder, and the elbow is there.
And when they roll away from both, the grip goes with them.
The fourth exit, once the arm is out and across.
Back: what the other three exist to set up.
When the neck is defended with both hands, the legs finish it.
And two hands on the neck means an arm is unattended.

items.title: Back → mount
items.notes: The exit that is not a finish. It is milestone 6's Back Control to Mount, named again here because a submission system that ends when they escape is not a system — the mount is where the next one starts.

phases.title: Leg Entanglement System
phases.description: Guard → leg entanglement → submission, or sweep, or back take, or come on top. Positional leg locking, not just submissions.

items.notes: The entry that turns a guard into an entanglement without a scramble.
The saddle, and the position the rest of this milestone is played from.
The finish that is legal where the heel hook is not.
Where the rules allow it — and the ruleset question is part of the technique.
The exit that is worth more than any of the finishes above.

items.title: Pass from them, sweep from them, come up
items.notes: An entanglement you can only submit from is a gamble. One you can also sweep, pass and take the back from is a position, and positions are what this belt is about.

phases.title: Scrambles and Wrestling
phases.description: Understand where the next dominant position will appear, and get there first.

items.notes: The wrestle-up: guard as a way to stand, not only a way to sweep.
Its gi version, which arrives with a grip already attached.
The mat return, so a scramble that ends standing does not end neutral.
The counter that turns their go-behind into your takedown.
Turtle attacks: what the position offers when you are the one on top of it.
And turtle recoveries, which is the same scramble read from underneath.

items.title: Scramble awareness
items.notes: A scramble is not chaos, it is a race to a position both of you can already see. The purple belt's edge is knowing which position that is one beat earlier.

phases.title: Strategy
phases.description: The part of the game that is decided before anyone touches anyone. None of this is a technique and none of it is counted — it is what the techniques are for.

items.title: Score
items.notes: What is the score, what does it make them do, and what does it let you refuse? A guard pull down four points is a different guard pull.

items.title: Time
items.notes: Two minutes left changes which risk is correct for each of you, and it changes it in opposite directions.

items.title: Risk
items.notes: Every attack has a cost if it fails. The question is never whether an attack is good, it is whether the position you land in when it fails is acceptable right now.

items.title: Energy
items.notes: Yours and theirs. A pace that beats them in round three is worth more than a technique that beats them in round one.

items.title: Opponent's strengths
items.notes: Where do they want this to go? Half of strategy is simply refusing to go there, which costs nothing and is rarely done.

items.title: Opponent's reactions
items.notes: The most valuable thing on this list. What do they do when you do X? Once that is known, everything above becomes arithmetic.

name: Brown belt: master your game
description: Goal: no longer learning every technique, but making fundamental BJJ extremely difficult to stop. Understand why, when, where and against whom a technique works. Almost nothing in this belt is new material — it is depth, answers and refinement, so nearly all of it is written rather than counted. The shape to hold in your head: control the initial engagement → force your preferred position → they react predictably → enter your A-game system → they defend → use the defence to advance → control the position → create multiple threats → finish. Or: they escape → immediately reconnect to another system → repeat.

phases.title: Create a Complete Starting Strategy
phases.description: Have an answer for each of the seven people you will actually meet, and several ways to dictate where the match happens.

items.title: Against a wrestler
items.notes: They want it standing and they are better at it. The question is whether you contest that or skip it, and either answer is fine as long as it was decided beforehand.

items.title: Against a guard puller
items.notes: They will sit down. What you do in the second after that decides the match — engage, disengage, or make them stand back up.

items.title: Against a bigger opponent
items.notes: Angles and distance rather than frames and pressure. Anything that becomes a contest of position-holding is a contest you have chosen to lose.

items.title: Against a smaller opponent
items.notes: They are faster and they will scramble. Weight and connection, and refuse the scramble rather than winning it.

items.title: Against a pressure player
items.notes: Do not let it start. Pressure games are much easier to prevent than to escape, which is a statement about where your effort should go.

items.title: Against a flexible guard player
items.notes: Their retention is better than your passing. Attack the connections and the grips rather than the legs.

items.title: Against a leg-lock player
items.notes: Know the knee line better than they do, and decide in advance which entanglements you will accept.

items.title: Multiple ways to dictate
items.notes: A single game plan is a game plan they can prepare for. The brown belt's real advantage is having three, and choosing between them in the first thirty seconds.

phases.title: Master Your Best Takedown System
phases.description: A deep system around two or three, rather than ten average takedowns. Single leg → they sprawl → front headlock; they pull the leg away → double leg; they whizzer → body lock; they turn → back take.

items.notes: The finish for the sprawl, so the shot is not abandoned.
And the finish for when they stay upright instead.
What the cleared leg hands you, taken without a reset.
The throw that answers the whizzer, because the whizzer commits their hips.
And the ending for all of it: their turn is not an escape.

items.title: Two or three, all the way down
items.notes: Ten takedowns is ten shallow trees. Two with every branch answered is what beats somebody who wrestles better than you.

phases.title: Master Your Primary Guard
phases.description: Answers against every major passing style. Not a technique list — a checklist you should be able to answer out loud for the one guard you actually play.

items.title: When they kneel
items.notes: The passer on their knees is playing a pressure game. What is your answer before the weight settles?

items.title: When they stand
items.notes: Standing removes your frames' leverage and adds their mobility. Most guards have one honest answer here and it is worth knowing which.

items.title: When they pressure pass
items.notes: The answer is almost never more frame. It is usually an angle, taken earlier than feels necessary.

items.title: When they body lock
items.notes: The narrowest window in passing. Either you break the connection before it closes, or you are playing a different game.

items.title: When they knee cut
items.notes: The most common pass in the sport. If you do not have two answers to it, you do not yet have a primary guard.

items.title: When they toreando
items.notes: Speed beats structure here, so the answer is rotation. Anybody who tries to out-grip a toreando loses slowly.

items.title: When they back step
items.notes: The pass that goes backwards, and the one guard players most often have no answer to because it does not look like a pass.

items.title: When they leg drag
items.notes: Already past you when you notice it. The answer is a decision — spin back or take the turtle deliberately.

items.title: When they attack your legs
items.notes: A passer who enters an entanglement has changed the game. Know the knee line from underneath as well as on top.

items.title: When they disengage
items.notes: They stand up and back away. This is a scoring question and a patience question, and it is the one most people have never thought about.

phases.title: Remove Guard Weaknesses
phases.description: If the primary guard fails → secondary guard → half guard → turtle → wrestle up → return to top. There should always be another layer.

items.title: The layers, in order
items.notes: Nothing here is a failure state. Each layer is a position with its own attacks, and the athlete who treats half guard or turtle as an emergency is the one who gets passed from them.
The layer almost everything falls back to, so it has to be genuinely good.
Turtle as a route back up rather than a place to wait.
And the wrestle-up, which is what turns the last layer into a top position.

items.title: There is always another layer
items.notes: The purpose is not that every layer works. It is that losing one is never the end of the sequence, so nothing you do from the bottom is ever a gamble on a single answer.

phases.title: Master a Passing Philosophy
phases.description: Understand why passes work — control the feet, then the knees, then the hips, then the shoulders, then the head — and have a complete system against each guard you will meet.

items.title: The order is the philosophy
items.notes: Feet, knees, hips, shoulders, head. Every pass that works is that order; every pass that fails skipped a step. This is the single sentence the rest of this milestone is an application of.

items.title: Against seated guard
items.notes: They have their hands and their base. The work happens before you are in range.

items.title: Against supine guard
items.notes: They have their legs and their hips, and you have your weight. Distance is the whole contest.

items.title: Against half guard
items.notes: Where most passes stall, and the one where the underhook decides everything.

items.title: Against butterfly
items.notes: Do not let them get underneath you. Everything butterfly does needs elevation and elevation needs space.

items.title: Against De La Riva
items.notes: Their hook is a lever on your base. Clear the hook or take the leg away — arguing with it in place is how you get swept.

items.title: Against lasso
items.notes: Your arm is theirs until you get it back. Passing before the arm is free is passing with one arm.

items.title: Against X guard
items.notes: Already underneath you. The answer is usually the ground, not more base.

items.title: Against inverted guards
items.notes: They will be facing away and moving. Passing is a matter of following the hips rather than beating the legs.

items.title: Against wrestle-up guards
items.notes: They do not want to sweep you, they want to stand. Treat it as a takedown defence problem and it becomes simple.

phases.title: Master Pinning
phases.description: Force defensive reactions rather than simply holding. Side control pressure → they frame → north-south → they turn → take the back. Or: mount → they protect the neck → separate the elbow → armbar → they hide the arm → gift wrap → back take.

items.notes: The first chain's ending, and the reason the frame was worth provoking.
The second chain's hinge: the elbow separated from the body.
What the separated elbow becomes.
And what hiding the arm becomes, which is worse for them than the armbar was.

items.title: A pin is a question you ask repeatedly
items.notes: Holding a pin invites them to work. Threatening from it forces a reaction, and the reaction is the transition. The brown belt rarely holds anything still.

phases.title: Develop Finishing Systems
phases.description: Four families. Each is a position with several finishes hanging off it rather than a finish you happen to know — and the point of a family is that they cannot defend all of it with the two hands they have. Every lesson below is one the document names, in the order it names them.

items.notes: Back: the one everything else in this family exists to set up.
What the hand fight leaves you when the RNC is denied.
When the neck is defended with both hands, the legs finish it.
And both hands on the neck means an arm is unattended.
The exit that is not a finish: a back escape is not an escape if you are already mounting them.
Mount: the choke that makes them turn.
The straight arm, taken before they can bend it back in.
And the triangle that arrives when they defend the arm triangle.

items.title: Mount: the back take
items.notes: The fourth exit, and it is the gift wrap from milestone 6 rather than a second technique — which is the point. A finishing family does not end at a submission; it ends wherever they are worst off, and from mount that is usually behind them.
Front headlock: the finish they expect, kept honest by the three below it.
When they turn in.
When they turn away.
And when they do neither, go behind. The unglamorous exit is the highest-percentage one.
Legs: the one that is legal everywhere, and the entry to the rest.
Where the ruleset allows it.
The finish that answers a defended heel exposure.
Where the rules allow it — and knowing which rules is part of the technique.
The entanglement is a position, so it sweeps as well as it finishes.
And the exit worth more than any finish above it.

phases.title: Master Defensive Layers
phases.description: The best defense is increasingly preventative. Six stages, and the earlier you act the cheaper it is.

items.title: Before control happens
items.notes: The cheapest layer and the one most people skip entirely. Almost every pin you escape was one you could have prevented for a fraction of the effort.

items.title: During control
items.notes: Frames, hips and the decision about which direction you are going before they have settled.

items.title: Before submission isolation
items.notes: The moment an arm or the neck becomes available is the moment to act. After this point every layer costs more.

items.title: During submission
items.notes: Structure rather than strength: the grip, the angle, the direction of the turn.

items.title: Late-stage escape
items.notes: It exists, it works more often than people think, and it should never be your first line.

items.title: Counterattack
items.notes: The layer that turns defence into offence, and the one that separates a brown belt from a very good blue belt.

phases.title: Control Scrambles
phases.description: Know when to scramble and, more importantly, when to stop. Every option below is a decision rather than a reflex.

items.title: When to scramble
items.notes: When the position you would land in is better than the one you are in, and when you are the one who can see it first.

items.title: When to stop scrambling
items.notes: When neither of those is true. Stopping is a skill and it is almost never taught.
Turtle: the decision to take it, made deliberately rather than arrived at.

items.title: When to wrestle
items.notes: Standing is a scramble too, and the same question applies with higher stakes.
Sit to guard: the reset that costs nothing when the scramble is not going your way.
Attack the front headlock: where most scrambles hand you a position if you are ready for it.
Chase the back: the scramble's best possible ending.

items.title: Stabilize position
items.notes: The unglamorous one, and usually the correct one. A scramble that ends in a stable pin has been won regardless of how it looked.

phases.title: Strategic Mastery
phases.description: Five questions. A brown belt should be able to answer all five about a specific opponent before the match, and about themselves at any moment during it.

items.title: Where do I want this fight?
items.notes: Standing, in your guard, in their guard, or on top. If the honest answer is "wherever it goes", that is the thing to fix first.

items.title: What is my strongest path there?
items.notes: Not the shortest and not the most impressive. The one that works when you are tired and they are ready for it.

items.title: What is my opponent likely to do?
items.notes: Most people have two answers to any given situation and you can find out which within a minute.

items.title: What is my answer?
items.notes: Prepared beforehand, not improvised. This is the difference between reacting well and having already decided.

items.title: What happens if my first strategy fails?
items.notes: The question that makes the other four worth asking. A plan with no second branch is a hope.

name: White belt: the whole list
description: Everything a white belt is working toward, in the order a round actually happens: standing, to the ground, guard, the pass, the pins, the back, and then how to get out of all of it. Nothing here is scored and nothing here completes — this is the reference you consult, not the path you work. The white belt ROADMAP is the path, and it is deliberately shorter.

phases.title: Start Standing
phases.description: Every round begins here, and the first job is not a takedown — it is being hard to move, hard to grip, and safe when you land. Nothing in this section scores a point and all of it decides whether the rest of the round happens on your terms.

items.notes: Knees bent, back straight, weight between your feet.
Whoever gets their hands inside decides what happens next.
In the gi, a collar and a sleeve is worth more than being stronger.
Learn to land before you learn to be thrown.
The other half of the same skill.
How you get up without giving your back or your legs.
The answer to a leg attack, and the first thing to drill until it is a reflex.

items.title: Posture is the whole game up here
items.notes: Bent over is where snapdowns, front headlocks and guillotines come from. Head up and back straight costs nothing and removes half of what they can do.

phases.title: Get the Fight to the Ground
phases.description: Two or three takedowns you understand beats ten you have seen. The goal is one attack you can finish, one you can stop, and a way to the floor that is yours rather than theirs.

items.notes: The one everybody learns, and it still works.
The other half of the pair — they defend one by giving you the other.
No level change, no scramble, and it travels to no-gi.
What their bad posture is for.
Pulling guard is a decision, not a surrender — but only if you choose the position.
The other one worth having, and safer on the knees.

items.title: Pick two and keep them
items.notes: A white belt with two takedowns they finish is ahead of one with eight they start. The rest of this list is here so you recognise what is being done to you.

phases.title: Understand Guard
phases.description: Guard is the only bottom position that attacks, and the thing that makes it a guard rather than being underneath somebody is that your legs are between you and them. Everything below is one way of keeping them there.

items.notes: Break their posture and most of their options go with it.
The grip that stops them stacking and sets up half the attacks.
Open guard starts with the hands, not the feet.
The close-range guard, and the one that lifts.
Half guard is a position with its own fight, not a failed guard.
Legs pummel like arms do; whoever gets inside keeps the guard.
The movement every recovery is built from.

items.title: Distance, then frames, then hips
items.notes: In that order, every time. Frames buy the space, hips use it. Reaching for a grip before you have either is how a guard gets passed.

phases.title: Sweep From Bottom
phases.description: If you cannot submit them safely, improve your position — that is the whole rule, and a sweep is how it is done from underneath. Two you can hit is a real white belt game.

items.notes: The first one most people land in a live round.
Pairs with the kimura: the defence to one is the entry to the other.
Also called the pendulum; it takes the arm with it.
The same family, from the other side.
Distance guard, standing opponent — the one that works when they stand up.
Close range, hooks in, and the whole body does the work.
The underhook, cashed in.

items.title: A sweep is a trade, not a trick
items.notes: You are exchanging their base for yours. Every one of these works by taking away a post and loading the direction they cannot post in.

phases.title: Pass the Guard From Top
phases.description: Before you can attack, the legs have to stop being between you. Passing is a sequence and skipping a step is why passes fail: legs, then hips, then shoulders, then the pin.

items.notes: You cannot pass a closed guard; you open it first, standing.
The kneeling alternative, for when standing is not on.
The pass that works in both gi and no-gi and never stops working.
Control the legs, move around them — the fast one.
Heavy, slow, and very hard to recover against.
The other pressure pass, and the one that beats a knee shield.
Half guard is where most passes stall; this is how they finish.
A place to pass FROM, so you stop starting from scratch each time.

items.title: A pass is not finished until the pin is
items.notes: Getting past the legs and stopping there is how you end up back in guard. The pass ends when side control is locked, not when the legs are cleared.

phases.title: Establish Side Control
phases.description: Where a finished pass lands, and the junction everything above it is reached from. Hold it first; the submissions are what their escape attempts hand you.

items.notes: The two grips that make the pin a pin.
Mobile, heavy, and worth points.
The first upgrade.
The second, and the one that keeps you moving.
Where side control goes when they turn in.
The arm they push with is the arm you take.
The other side of the same arm.

items.title: Chest to chest, hips to the mat
items.notes: Weight goes through your chest onto theirs, not through your knees onto the floor. A pin that feels heavy to you and light to them is not a pin.

phases.title: Establish Mount
phases.description: Stabilise before you attack. Almost every lost mount is somebody reaching for a submission from a mount that was not finished.

items.notes: Hips low, feet hooked, and very hard to bridge.
Climb when they turn: high mount is where the attacks live.
The step between holding and finishing.
Separate the arm before you need it.
The first submission most people land from the top.
The gi choke that is worth the years it takes.
The one that works when they have hidden their neck.
What the arm they defend the choke with is for.
The simpler version, and often the faster one.

phases.title: Take and Control the Back
phases.description: The best place in the sport, and the only one they cannot see. It is also the one position where control and submission are nearly the same skill.

items.notes: One arm over, one under. Never both over.
The legs that stop them turning.
Where the back goes when they escape it well.
The submission that needs no gi, no strength and no mistake from them.
The gi equivalent, and it arrives sooner.

items.title: Follow, do not hold
items.notes: Back control is not a grip, it is a chase. When they turn, you turn with them and keep your chest on their back — squeezing harder while they rotate is how the position is lost.

phases.title: Turtle
phases.description: A door, never a room. Turtle is somewhere you move through — and on top, it is the shortest path to the back there is.

items.notes: Neck first, always.
The way out that puts you back on the bottom of guard.
The other way out, under them.
And the way out that ends standing.
On top: the same grip as back control, taken earlier.
How the seatbelt becomes the back.

items.title: Staying still in turtle is volunteering your back
items.notes: There is no defensive turtle that holds. Every second spent waiting there is a second they are using to get a hook in.

phases.title: Escape Bad Positions
phases.description: The largest section at this belt, and it should be. A white belt who escapes well is dangerous at blue; one who only attacks is starting over.

items.notes: Survive first. Escapes come after the danger is off.
When they reach, you roll them.
When they do not, you shrimp out.
Frames are what make being pinned uncomfortable rather than dangerous.
The standard escape, and the one everything else falls back to.
The other direction: up, not out.
Two hands to your neck before anything else.
Escape toward the side without their arm under it.
Get your shoulders to the floor and the position is already half gone.
Peel a hook and they lose the legs that hold you.

items.title: Survive, escape, recover — in that order
items.notes: Trying to escape while a choke is still live is how people get finished. Take the danger off first; the position will still be there.

phases.title: Submission Defense
phases.description: Submission defence at this belt is mostly recognition. You do not need to escape everything — you need to know what is happening early enough to do something, and late enough to tap without an injury.

items.notes: The one you must recognise instantly, because the late version does not work.

items.title: Tap early, tap often
items.notes: A tap costs you thirty seconds. An arm costs you six months. Nobody in the room remembers who tapped; everybody remembers who trains hurt.

items.title: The three you must recognise
items.notes: Anything on your neck, anything straightening your arm, and anything twisting your knee. The first two you have time for. The third you do not — knees give with no warning, which is why heel hooks are not a white belt problem to solve, they are one to avoid.

items.title: Position first, then defence
items.notes: Almost every submission needs a position to work from. Escaping the position early is easier than escaping the submission late, every time.

name: Blue belt: the whole list
description: The full blue belt reference, in match order. The change this belt asks for runs through all of it: every technique is half of a pair, and the other half is what they do to defend the first. Nothing here is scored — the blue belt roadmap is the worked path through this material.

phases.title: Standing
phases.description: One takedown fails against anybody good. Blue belt wrestling is the second attempt arriving before the first has finished failing.

items.notes: The inside single, for when the outside one is defended.
The double as a finish to a failed single, not as a first move.
The third angle on the same leg.
What a whizzer hands you.
The entry that costs nothing and threatens the back.
A grip that is a takedown, a sweep and a submission at once.
Behind them is not finished until they are down.
The other way to finish from behind.
Pulling into a guard you actually play.
And pulling straight into a leg entry.

items.title: Attack in twos
items.notes: Single leg into double, snapdown into go-behind, collar tie into arm drag. Pick pairs where their defence to the first IS the opening for the second.

phases.title: Guard Retention
phases.description: Retention is a ladder you fall down in order — distance, foot frames, knee frames, hand frames, hips, then late recovery. A guard is hard to pass when losing one rung just means arriving at the next.

items.notes: The rung most people skip.
The one below the hips, and it is not optional at blue.
Recovering under them rather than away from them.
Against the pass you will meet most.
Against the one that beats a lazy frame.
The last rung before turtle.

items.title: Losing a rung is not losing the guard
items.notes: Every pass is a sequence too. Interrupt it at any step and they start again — which is why retention is a ladder rather than a wall.

phases.title: Build Two Guards
phases.description: Not every open guard: two, chosen so the other answers what beats the first. Long range and close range is the usual pairing.

items.notes: The long-range hook, and the entry to most of the rest.
The sweep that punishes a standing passer.
And the one that punishes a kneeling one.
Close range, and the strongest lifting position on the bottom.
The back take that lives inside butterfly.
The hinge between the two ranges.
The gi version of the same idea.
And the one that stops a passer moving at all.

items.title: A guard you play on purpose
items.notes: The change at this belt is choosing where the fight happens instead of reacting to where it went.

phases.title: Attack From Guard
phases.description: At white belt the closed-guard attacks were separate answers. Now they are one question asked three ways: the defence to each is the entry to the next.

items.notes: The centre of the chain.
Where the triangle goes when they posture out.
And where the armbar goes when they pull the arm.
The sweep and the submission that share a grip.
The exit nobody defends.
Half guard becomes profitable, not just survivable.
And the same grip takes the back.
The engine underneath when the underhook stalls.

items.title: Three attacks, one grip
items.notes: Triangle, armbar and omoplata are the same position seen from three angles. Learning them as one thing is the point of this belt.

phases.title: Develop Passing Systems
phases.description: A passing system needs a fast answer and a heavy one, and they share a structure: control the feet or knees, set the angle, defeat the frames, then the hips, then the shoulders, then stabilise.

items.notes: The movement pass that ends facing their back.
And what it turns into when they turn away.
The other movement pass, and the simplest to drill.
The heavy one, and very hard to frame against.
Its answer to a knee in the way.
Pressure through half guard rather than around it.
The knee shield is the wall this belt learns to climb.
Two passes as one movement.
The reaction map, written as a sequence.

items.title: Combine them
items.notes: Toreando, they recover; knee cut, they block; leg drag. One pass is a technique — three that feed each other is a system.

phases.title: Control After Passing
phases.description: Connect the pins instead of holding one forever: side control, north-south, knee-on-belly, mount and back are one position seen from five angles. Absent from the old syllabus phase list entirely; backfilled from the roadmap milestone of the same name (N110/F28 reconciliation).

items.notes: The pin you land in, and the one everything below leaves from.
The head switch that answers their first frame.
Lighter and more mobile, and it makes them give you something.
When their frames go to your hips, mount is on the other side of them.
And when they turn instead, the back is already exposed.

items.title: A pin is a place you leave
items.notes: Not a destination. The athlete who transitions on every frame is much harder to escape than the one who squeezes harder.

phases.title: Build Submission Chains
phases.description: Blue-belt pins are dynamic: side control, knee on belly, north–south and mount are one position seen from four angles, and the submissions live in the transitions between them.

items.notes: The grip that makes the back inevitable.
The kimura as a control, not a finish.
The one submission that is easier from north–south.
What their frame hands you.
And what their turn hands you.
The mount that follows them instead of resisting.
Mount to back, without a scramble.
The attack they walk into while defending the choke.
The gi finish that ends most blue belt rounds.
And the no-gi one.

phases.title: Front Headlock
phases.description: Every snapdown, every stuffed shot and every duck-out lands here. At blue it stops being a place you hold a neck and becomes a position with exits.

items.notes: Control first. The chokes only work from a headlock that already holds.
The one everybody meets first.
For when their arm is in.
And the roll that goes with it.
The exit that is not a submission, and usually the right one.
Turning a turtle into a back take.

items.title: The go-behind is the default
items.notes: A choke that fails from here costs you the position. Taking the back from a front headlock costs nothing and is worth more.

phases.title: Leg Locks
phases.description: Leg locks start with positional responsibility, not submissions: control the position, know the rule set, and protect your partners. The straight ankle is the whole family in miniature.

items.notes: The entanglement everything else is built from.
The one legal at every belt, and the one to learn properly.
The entanglement as a sweep, which is what it mostly is.
The other direction.
Where the knee line is, and why it decides everything.
Getting out, which you will need first.

items.title: The knee line is the whole rule
items.notes: If their knee is past your centre they control the entanglement, whatever your grips say. Learn to recognise it before you learn any finish.

items.title: Heel hooks are a rule-set question, not a skill question
items.notes: They are illegal in most gi competition below brown and legal in most no-gi. Know which room you are in, and never crank one in training.

phases.title: Improve Escapes
phases.description: White belt escapes were single answers. Blue belt escapes are sequences: they block the first, which opens the second.

items.notes: Elbow escape, they block, bridge, they post, half guard.
The escape that works after the easy window closed.
Against the mount that followed you.
The second answer when frames alone fail.
Turtle as a deliberate choice, not a collapse.
For when the early defence was already missed.
The gi choke most likely to catch you at this belt.
And the trap that catches people defending well.

name: Purple belt: the whole list
description: The purple belt reference. Less new material than any belt before it and more connective tissue: entries, back takes underneath, entanglements as positions, and a game named out loud. Nothing here is scored.

phases.title: Establish a Standing Game
phases.description: The standing game the roadmap names directly: know which exit you are hunting -- guillotine or back take -- before the shot goes in, or pull straight into an attack instead. Absent from the old syllabus phase list entirely; backfilled from the roadmap milestone of the same name (N110/F28 reconciliation).

items.notes: The finish that answers the sprawl instead of abandoning the leg.
Where the failed single leg is supposed to arrive.
Or pull, and pull directly into an attack.

items.title: Know what you want before it starts
items.notes: Decided, not discovered. The purple belt's edge over the blue belt is rarely a better single leg -- it is having decided what the sprawl was going to turn into before shooting.

phases.title: Build an A-Game Guard
phases.description: A developed guard is an entry system, retention, sweeps, back takes, wrestle-ups and leg entries that all start from the same grips.

items.notes: The entry.
The wrestle-up.
The back take.
The neighbouring entry, for when they stand.
The entry underneath, when they stand tall.
The connection between the two.

items.title: Same grips, five outcomes
items.notes: The mark of a developed guard is that sweeping, submitting, taking the back and standing up all begin identically. They cannot defend the first move if it does not tell them which one is coming.

phases.title: Build Guard Connections
phases.description: Purple guard play points at the back: the berimbolo and crab-ride family turn a defended sweep into an arrival behind them.

items.notes: Expensive to learn, and worth it.
The cheaper half, and often the one that lands.
The other route to the same place.
And its finish.
The back take that reads as a scramble.

phases.title: Advanced Guard Retention
phases.description: Advanced retention is retention against a plan: against leg drags, body locks, floating passers and your own fatigue.

items.notes: Now a rung you use, not one you fall to.
Recovering into an attack rather than into a reset.
Against the pass that gives you no frames.
Turtle as a transitional guard.
And turtle as an attack.

phases.title: Build a Passing Tree
phases.description: Advanced passing reads reactions instead of forcing outcomes: weight on their knees, direction changes off their answers, and a map of where each defence sends you.

items.notes: Weight without commitment, which is what makes it float.
The direction change.
Where a turn away sends you.
The chain, as one movement.
And the version that skips side control entirely.

phases.title: Control Transitions
phases.description: Advanced control makes every escape attempt cost something: the pin follows them, and each defensive turn exposes the next attack.

items.notes: Their turn, taken.
The cycle that never gives the position back.
The control that holds through a scramble.
The one that turns a turtle into two trapped arms.
And its finish.

phases.title: Develop Submission Systems
phases.description: Two systems that both end at the back: the front headlock, the junction every stuffed shot and duck-out lands in, and the kimura, a grip that outlives whatever position it started in. Merged from the old syllabus's separate "The front headlock system" and "The kimura as a system" phases so the syllabus carries one phase per roadmap milestone (N110/F28 reconciliation) -- no item from either was dropped.

items.notes: The darce from the pin rather than the scramble.
The version that finishes on a defended neck.
Their wrestle-up, answered.
The roll, and when not to take it.
The back take.
From underneath.
The finish, when it is there.
The pass nobody expects from a submission grip.

items.title: A grip that outlives the position
items.notes: Every other control here is lost when the position changes. This one is not, which is why it is worth years.

phases.title: Leg Entanglement System
phases.description: Purple treats entanglements the way white treated pins: positions with controls, escapes and exchanges, not lotteries.

items.notes: The entry that changes what is available.
The finish that does not need a heel.
Where the rules allow it.
The position both people are in at once.
Answering an entry with an entry.

items.title: Pass from them, sweep from them, come up
items.notes: A submission is one of four exits. Treating the entanglement as a position is what makes the other three available.

phases.title: Scrambles and Wrestling
phases.description: A scramble is not chaos — it is a race with rules: hips lower than theirs, head on the winning side, and a known exit.

items.notes: The scramble you start on purpose.
The one that ends behind them.
And the one that ends on your feet.

items.title: Know your exit before you start
items.notes: The person who wins a scramble is usually the one who knew where it was going. Entering one to see what happens is how positions are lost.

phases.title: Strategy
phases.description: Purple belt starts with an architecture, written down: a primary standing entry, a primary guard, a secondary guard that solves the primary's problems, a passing system and a finishing system.

items.title: Write it down
items.notes: If you cannot say your game in five lines, you do not have one yet — you have a collection. The phases below are the five lines.

items.title: The question changes
items.notes: It stops being what do I do here and becomes which reaction do I want. Everything below is a way of asking for one.

name: Brown belt: the whole list
description: The brown belt reference, and the shortest of the four on purpose — most of what a brown belt knows is on the three lists below this one, held to a standard nobody applies at blue. What IS new is largely the leg family and the finishes that need somebody else's mistake to be small. Nothing here is scored.

phases.title: Create a Complete Starting Strategy
phases.description: Have an answer for each of the seven people you will actually meet, and several ways to dictate where the match happens. Absent from the old syllabus phase list entirely; backfilled verbatim from the roadmap milestone of the same name (N110/F28 reconciliation) -- these are concepts, not techniques, so roadmap and syllabus read identically here.

items.title: Almost nothing here is new
items.notes: This syllabus lists material you have had for years. What changes is the standard: against the best person in the room, when tired, when they know what is coming.

items.title: Against a wrestler
items.notes: They want it standing and they are better at it. The question is whether you contest that or skip it, and either answer is fine as long as it was decided beforehand.

items.title: Against a guard puller
items.notes: They will sit down. What you do in the second after that decides the match -- engage, disengage, or make them stand back up.

items.title: Against a bigger opponent
items.notes: Angles and distance rather than frames and pressure. Anything that becomes a contest of position-holding is a contest you have chosen to lose.

items.title: Against a smaller opponent
items.notes: They are faster and they will scramble. Weight and connection, and refuse the scramble rather than winning it.

items.title: Against a pressure player
items.notes: Do not let it start. Pressure games are much easier to prevent than to escape, which is a statement about where your effort should go.

items.title: Against a flexible guard player
items.notes: Their retention is better than your passing. Attack the connections and the grips rather than the legs.

items.title: Against a leg-lock player
items.notes: Know the knee line better than they do, and decide in advance which entanglements you will accept.

items.title: Multiple ways to dictate
items.notes: A single game plan is a game plan they can prepare for. The brown belt's real advantage is having three, and choosing between them in the first thirty seconds.

phases.title: Master Your Best Takedown System
phases.description: Two or three attacks with every counter-reaction mapped, rather than ten average ones.

items.notes: The centre of most systems, because everything answers it.
For the sprawl.
For the whizzer.
For the leg they pull away.
For the turn.
And one throw, because a system with no throw is readable.

phases.title: Master Your Primary Guard
phases.description: Your A-game guard needs an answer to every major passing style, and a second layer under it when it fails.

items.notes: Against a kneeling passer.
Against a standing one.
Against pressure.
Against a leg drag.
Against a body lock.
And the deliberate choice of turtle over a compromised guard.

phases.title: Remove Guard Weaknesses
phases.description: If the primary guard fails -> secondary guard -> half guard -> turtle -> wrestle up -> return to top. Absent from the old syllabus phase list entirely; backfilled from the roadmap milestone of the same name (N110/F28 reconciliation).

items.notes: The layer almost everything falls back to, so it has to be genuinely good.
Turtle as a route back up, not a place to wait.
And the wrestle-up, which turns the last layer into a top position.

items.title: There is always another layer
items.notes: Losing one is never the end of the sequence, so nothing you do from the bottom is ever a gamble on a single answer.

phases.title: Master a Passing Philosophy
phases.description: Understand why passes work -- control the feet, then the knees, then the hips, then the shoulders, then the head -- and have a complete system against each guard you will meet. Absent from the old syllabus phase list entirely; backfilled verbatim from the roadmap milestone of the same name (N110/F28 reconciliation) -- these are concepts, not techniques, so roadmap and syllabus read identically here.

items.title: The order is the philosophy
items.notes: Feet, knees, hips, shoulders, head. Every pass that works is that order; every pass that fails skipped a step.

items.title: Against seated guard
items.notes: They have their hands and their base. The work happens before you are in range.

items.title: Against supine guard
items.notes: They have their legs and their hips, and you have your weight. Distance is the whole contest.

items.title: Against half guard
items.notes: Where most passes stall, and the one where the underhook decides everything.

items.title: Against butterfly
items.notes: Do not let them get underneath you. Everything butterfly does needs elevation and elevation needs space.

items.title: Against De La Riva
items.notes: Their hook is a lever on your base. Clear the hook or take the leg away -- arguing with it in place is how you get swept.

items.title: Against lasso
items.notes: Your arm is theirs until you get it back. Passing before the arm is free is passing with one arm.

items.title: Against X guard
items.notes: Already underneath you. The answer is usually the ground, not more base.

items.title: Against inverted guards
items.notes: They will be facing away and moving. Passing is a matter of following the hips rather than beating the legs.

items.title: Against wrestle-up guards
items.notes: They do not want to sweep you, they want to stand. Treat it as a takedown defence problem and it becomes simple.

phases.title: Master Pinning
phases.description: Instead of holding a position, make every escape attempt cost something.

items.notes: Their frame, punished.
Their hidden arm, punished.
The control that survives their best escape.
And the one nobody trains against.

phases.title: Develop Finishing Systems
